subject: beekeeper
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: beekeeper with smoker and hive.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm brainstorming distinctive visual styles for this TypeScript module—considering options like folk-art tin toy, illuminated manuscript marginalia, constructivist poster, or stained-glass with bold lead lines and saturated flat colors.

Eventually I settle on Khokhloma, a Russian lacquerware tradition using glossy black backgrounds with red and gold floral swirls, picturing the beekeeper as a lathe-turned wooden figure painted in this style, with the hive and bees rendered in matching gold-and-black patterns and floral SVG textures.

Now I'm working out the layout: a chunky, toy-like humanoid around 1.5m tall with an oversized veiled head, holding a smoker, positioned slightly off-center alongside a painted hive box so the overall composition balances near the origin.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure: hips as root, a spine chain, neck, head, and jaw joint. For the veil, I'm considering a net-like texture with alpha cutouts applied to a cylinder or lathe mesh so it reads as mesh fabric rather than solid.

For the face itself, I'm thinking a Khokhloma-style painted decal with simple features — eyes, brows, nose, rosy cheeks, mustache — applied to a skull sphere, with the jaw as a separate lower piece holding the mouth decal so the head splits naturally at the joint.

I'm settling on the Khokhloma palette: deep black lacquer, red, gold, cream, and a touch of green. For the beekeeper coat, I want a cream-white base decorated with gold-red floral trim panels on the front and back, achieved via SVG decals rather than textures, giving it that traditional lacquerware look.

Now I'm working out the figure's proportions for a chunky toy-like beekeeper around 1.55m tall, blocking out key heights for boots, legs, hips, and torso so the body reads as sturdy and doll-like, with the hat, boots, and gloves also styled in the same black-red-cream lacquer scheme.

Continuing up, I settle the neck, head, and hat heights to bring the total figure to roughly 1.8m with the brim and crown stacked on top. For the rest pose, I'm deciding on a loose A-pose with arms angled slightly outward from the body, and working out where to hang the smoker from one hand so the bellows and nozzle read naturally at the figure's side.

I'm placing the smoker's can and conical nozzle relative to the hand's grip point, with the bellows handle positioned behind the can so the body sticks forward slightly from the hand, letting the arm hang just a touch forward to accommodate it.

Actually, for the rest pose I'll keep both arms symmetrical in a neutral A-pose rather than differing, with the right hand's fingers curled around the smoker's handle grip.

Still defining arm joint positions...

Rather than fussing with a handle threaded through fingers, I'll give both hands a modest curl so the right hand looks like it's loosely gripping the smoker handle without needing precise alignment.

I'll settle on curled fingers forming a loose fist around the bellows handle peg, and to keep the pose readable I'll curve the fingers similarly in both hands rather than making one open and one closed.

I'm reconsidering the grip geometry entirely—rather than a vertical peg, maybe a horizontal handle like a suitcase grip makes more sense, where the hand hangs down and fingers curl around it toward the palm.

Actually, I think smokers are often carried by a wire bail handle on top, like an old kettle, so the can hangs below with the bail arching over it, pivoting at the sides and gripped along the x-axis at the top. The bellows would attach to the back of the can.

I'm overthinking the hand-grip detail too much. I'll just settle on a simpler orientation: bail bar along z, arching in the yz plane with pivots front and back, keeping the bellows mounted on the side away from the hand.

I realize the forward-up nozzle would collide with an arch spanning the yz plane, so I'm reconsidering the bail shape: maybe pivots at the sides with uprights rising to a cross-bar, forming a U-shaped handle instead.

Simpler fix: put the bail bar along x at the lid's rear, so the spout which rises as it extends forward never enters the bail's plane near the lid top, avoiding collision entirely.

For the hand grip, I'll fudge it as a rigid pose rather than solving real anatomy — fingers curled forward wrapping over the bar with the wrist pronated so the palm faces back, keeping the hanging arm looking natural enough without exact joint rotations.

Working out finger curl geometry around the bar...

For the thumb I'm routing it from the palm side forward and up toward the bar, curled slightly. For the finger joint chains, I'll generate each with a seven-point catmull path and three joints per finger, then write a shared hand-building function parameterized by side and curl amount so the right hand grips the bar while the left hand rests in a relaxed, slightly curved pose—though I need to reconcile the mirroring since the right hand's palm orientation and finger spread won't directly mirror to the left.

I'm deciding to keep both hands in the same orientation, palm facing back with fingers spread and curling forward, but giving the left hand a looser curl since it's not holding anything, and softening the forward bend for an open look. I'm also placing the hands relative to the A-pose shoulder and wrist x-positions, with the bar sized to span near the hand width.

Now I'm working out the position of the can the right hand holds, pinning its center under the wrist and setting its top and bottom y-coordinates so it sits clear of the legs. I'm also figuring out the bail arch as a small half-circle pivoting from points just above the can's top center.

Still writing bail curve points...

Next I'm moving on to placing the bellows along the lateral side of the can near the left hand.

Reconsidering orientation: boards horizontal in the xz plane means the bellows opens vertically, so I'm placing the bottom board near y=0.35 and top near y=0.45 with tapered fold layers between them to simulate the accordion leather.

Now I'm thinking about the beehive separately: a Langstroth-style stack with stand legs, bottom board, two deep boxes with handle slots, a honey super, telescoping peaked-roof lid, an entrance landing board, and a few gold-bodied bees with wing cards floating around in flight.

For the hive boxes, I'm leaning into Khokhloma-style decoration -- black lacquer with red and gold floral panels on each side plus gold trim, and peeking honeycomb frames for detail. Scale-wise the hive sits around 0.5 wide by 0.4 deep, roughly 1.0 tall on its stand.

For the beekeeper, I'm planning accessories like a tool belt with a hive tool, a veiled hat, boots, an apron, and a few gold-dot bees crawling on the sleeve, with the left hand left open rather than holding anything. I'm also starting a list of around eight textures, beginning with a repeating red/gold floral band pattern to use as decal sprigs on the coat.

Now I'm mapping out the rest of that texture list -- a sprig design with gold stems and red berries for the coat, a hem border strip for trim bands, a veil net lattice, a facial feature set, a bee wing card, a bee emblem for the apron, a larger floral panel for the hive sides, and a honeycomb texture for the frame interiors.

9. Smoke puffs card: stylizing grey-cream smoke curls rising from the smoker nozzle using flattened, scaled spheres in pale grey-blue tones, plus an orange ember glow at the nozzle tip.
10. Planning hat band decals and labels, along with custom paint definitions for the black lacquer, red lacquer, and cream coat with warm/cool shading variation.

I'm thinking through the full Khokhloma lacquer-toy aesthetic: everything turned like a lathe, with the torso built as a pear-shaped bell-coat loft (like a matryoshka doll) sweeping from hips to chest into a flared beekeeper's smock, while keeping shared materials like wood grain, straw, and mottled leather within a limited flat color palette.

Working out the sweep path and radius profile for the torso—wide at the skirt bottom, narrowing at the waist, widening again at the chest before tapering to the shoulders, tied to a spine chain from hips to the neck joint.

To reduce risk, I could just make the torso rigid instead, but a smooth chain bending through the spine joints feels better, starting the path from the hips.

I'm structuring the spine as a chain from the hips up to the chest, then a follow-up neck chain from the chest up to the head, naming the intermediate joints so the tip lands correctly at chest and head.

Now I'm sketching the arm chains, parenting shoulders to the spine or chest and naming joints shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand with roles for arm, figuring out how tip naming works with path point counts.

For the legs I'm using hip, knee, ankle joints parented to hips with a leg role, then planning a separate toe joint for foot attachments.

Positions are mirrored on each side (left = +X), with hip near the top, knee in the middle, and ankle near the ground — boots will attach at the ankle and sit flush with the floor. For visuals, I'm giving the trousers a tapered sweep radius and sticking with a cream suit color with black boots for the beekeeper look.

Modeling boots as lathed cylinders with a red band near the top, plus a capsule-shaped foot piece swept from heel to toe, and a thin flat sole slab underneath for grounding.

I'm adding a small gold toe cap for decoration, then moving to the head: a peach-toned skull sphere with rosy cheeks in the Khokhloma-doll style, plus a separate jaw piece positioned as an ellipsoid joint below the face.

For the beard, I'm thinking of a bushy cream-gold Khokhloma-style design made of several overlapping tapered curl shapes swept along the jaw, colored with a root-to-tip gradient, visible through the transparent veil net, with a curled mustache made from two spiral sweeps. Next I'm working on the facial decal details, starting with round black eyes with white highlights.

Then I'm adding the hanging net veil beneath the brim as a tapered cylinder, patterned with a lattice texture that needs to wrap correctly around the geometry rather than repeat per face.

Working out the SVG viewBox dimensions and stroke widths for the lattice pattern...

The veil rides on the head bone and extends down past the shoulders, with the interior wall visible from inside and the back net showing the head silhouette behind it. For the hat, I'm planning a lacquered black brim with a red underside, gold trim and bead cord around the edge, tiny gold bee decals, and a golden "honey-drop" knob on the crown, with the brim surface painted using concentric rings based on distance from the center axis.

I'm shifting to the torso: a cream khokhloma-style coat with a red hem band and gold line near the bottom, red cuffs, chest and back sprig decals, and a circular bee emblem on an apron pocket, all projected onto the torso's surface sweep. I'm also adding a red lacquered collar ring with gold beads around the neck and sketching out a belt loop positioned at the hips.

To avoid messy horizontal offsets, I decide to keep the beekeeper centered at x=0 and instead place the hive in front along the z-axis, with the figure facing it — this keeps the whole composition's bounding box centered without needing lateral shifts.

Writing coordinate helper functions...

Now I'm planning the bees: around ten flying near the hive plus one on the hat or sleeve, each stylized larger than realistic scale with a gold-and-black striped body, small black head, and pale teardrop-shaped wings, while figuring out how to orient the stripe pattern correctly on each bee regardless of position.

Since hive parts need stable attachment points regardless of pose, I should add explicit joints for props like the hive and smoker, parented under hips, so they don't drift to unrelated nearest bones.

I'm sketching a helper pattern where part-building functions take a current bone context so props attach to the right joint — smoker parts to a hand joint, swarm/bee parts to the hive joint — with bone options threaded through all the geometry helpers like stick, sweep, extrude, and lathe. I'm now planning out the overall code structure before writing the roughly 800 lines needed.

Rather than risk importing a glow kit from an uncertain submodule path, I decide to implement my own glow helper that clones a part's material and bumps its emissive properties, carefully preserving texture maps when present — avoiding the import risk entirely while matching the kit's intended effect.

Now I'm confirming that all the builder helpers (createBuilder, frame, aim, rng, arc, bezier, paint, stripes, etc.) genuinely export from the single SDK module, then sketching out the color palette I'll use—blacks, reds, and gold tones for the lacquered look.

Finishing the palette with cream, skin, leather, wood, and bee-yellow hues, then starting to define paint helpers—like a lacquer function that mixes base and highlight colors with a soft gloss gradient for a warm sheen.

Still writing paint shaders...

Defining spine and torso sweep points...

Shoulders slope from wide at y=1.28 down to narrow at 1.34, with arms attaching at the sides and small cream spheres added as puffy shoulder pads. I'm setting flat caps at the hem for a clean lathe edge and round caps at the top, then mapping the sweep parameter to y using arc-length so the profile spacing stays even along the path.

Now I'm defining the skeleton structure: a spine/hips body chain, then leg bones tapering from thigh to knee to ankle with radii narrowing toward the boot shaft that covers the lower leg. The trousers stay mostly hidden by the coat and boots, visible only in a narrow band at the thigh, with the hip joint sitting inside the coat opening. For the arms I'm tapering the sleeve radius from shoulder to wrist for a baggy look, then adding a cuff band with cream, red, and gold color stops near the wrist.

For hands I'm sketching gauntlet cuffs with a red-lacquer flare at the wrist leading into a cream glove, computing the palm position by offsetting down from the wrist joint in world space since the arm isn't axis-aligned, with fingers spreading along the local x-axis.

Now I'm working through the arm geometry itself — placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist points, checking upper arm and forearm segment lengths, and shaping the A-pose angle so the bend looks natural.

Then I'm positioning the palm and fingers, calculating knuckle row offsets and a small bar element, and spacing out the four fingers evenly across the palm width before setting up the finger curl for the open hand pose.

Now I'm setting up the finger chain naming convention, using thumb, index, middle, ring, and pinky as distinct named joints parented to the wrist, each with its own three-joint chain.

For geometry, I'm defining a tapered finger radius profile and settling on a cream-gold glove color. I'm also designing a lathed gauntlet cuff flaring outward from the wrist along the forearm axis, with a gold trim ring, then planning the thumb's shorter two-joint chain branching off the palm.

Now I'm starting to write the actual builder code defining the beekeeper figure.

Still placing head and jaw joints...

I'm placing the mustache slightly below the nose, then positioning eye decals onto the skull surface using directional projection so they sit correctly on the curved face.

For the skull geometry itself, I'm deciding between a smooth lathe-turned wooden-toy look versus low-poly facets—leaning toward keeping it smooth but using a reduced segment count like 12×8 to stay stylistically consistent with a carved wooden figure.

Now I'm working out the hat shape as a lathed profile, placing the brim just above the eyes around y=1.64-1.66 so it doesn't obscure them, with the crown rising to about 1.80-1.82 total height. I'm defining the brim as a separate thin lathed disc with a slightly turned-down edge, outlining its radial profile points.

The brim's forward projection still leaves the eyes visible from a front view, so that checks out. Now I'm checking the veil, a cone from the brim edge down to the shoulders, making sure it clears the shoulder geometry.

Checking the chest and shoulder geometry, I lower the veil bottom to y 1.31 with height 0.34 so it clears the shoulder spheres cleanly. I'm also adding decorative rings—a red lacquer band swept around the veil bottom and a gold band near the brim, using a closed circular sweep for the torus shape.

I'm attaching the veil and hat to the head bone, then adding hat decorations: a red torus band with gold bee emblems, placing a decal badge at the crown front and figuring out radial ring patterns for the brim paint based on distance from the hat axis.

Writing brim paint logic...

For the beard, I'm sweeping seven blade shapes from the jaw's front-lower arc down and forward, computing anchor points analytically around the jaw curve with bezier controls tapering from wide to pointed tips, then coloring them with a cream-to-gold gradient.

For the mustache, I'm building curled bezier sweeps on each side starting near the nose base, curving outward and down before flicking upward, with thick roots tapering to fine tips in the same gold-cream palette, positioned so it naturally covers the mouth area below.

I'm checking the jaw-to-skull continuity at the face front, computing the ellipsoid radii at different y-heights to make sure the surface curves smoothly from skull to jaw without a visible seam, then placing a small mouth decal in the gap where the jaw curves inward.

Now I'm adding torso details like a belt with a leather band and gold buckle loop, positioning it around the waist where torso radius is roughly 0.19, and working out how to sweep a thin tube shape for the ring geometry.

I'm leaning toward a chunkier red lacquer sash with gold beads strung along its loop path, plus tassels hanging from a front-left knot built from cone and sphere shapes.

Now I'm adding a beaded collar at the neck base, visible faintly beneath the veil net, and sketching out the hive setup: a lathe-turned stand with legs in red and gold, a bottom board with a landing platform extending forward, and a top super left slightly open to reveal the frames inside.

I'm stacking the hive boxes with specific height ranges -- two deep brood boxes and a honey super -- topped with a gabled telescoping lid, bringing the whole hive to about waist-to-chest height on the 1.8-unit-tall beekeeper for a satisfyingly chunky proportion.

Each box is roughly 0.50 wide by 0.42 deep, painted with lacquer and detailed with framed floral decal panels, gold corner trim strips, and dark recessed handle slots with a gold lip. I'm placing a textured front panel as a thin plane layered just in front of the box surface to act as the decal.

I'm alternating lacquer colors between boxes (black with red-gold panels, red with black-gold panels), generating the panel textures procedurally, and now starting to extrude a gable-shaped roof profile for the hive lid.

Finishing the roof means adding gold trim and ridge detailing with striped shingle lines, then placing a bee emblem decal on the triangular front gable face.

I'm also planning a gold finial for the roof peak, a small entrance slot with a landing board trimmed in red for bees to approach, and amber honey-drip shapes dripping from the super's edge for a glossy lacquer finish.

Actually, I'll add a small glazed observation window on the super front with a glowing honeycomb texture and gold frame instead, which is a nicer use of the glow effect. I'm also setting up a hinge joint for the lid so the roof can open.

Now I'm moving on to the bees, designing a builder function that takes position, heading direction, and scale, starting with the abdomen as a scaled sphere with painted stripes.

I'll alternate the stripe colors based on a floor/modulo of the UV coordinate, switching between bee-yellow and black bands. For the bee itself, I'm scaling everything up 2.5x from real size, building the abdomen, a fuzzy dark-gold thorax offset toward the front, and a small black head sphere, while deciding whether tiny eye dots are worth the added complexity before moving on to wings.

Working out wing geometry...

I'll add a stinger spike, bringing bee part count to roughly 11-12 per bee, with wing color set to a pale blue. For the hat I'm adding a bee emblem texture, and for the smoker I'm planning rising smoke puffs as low-poly icospheres in grayish tones with an ember glow inside the nozzle, drifting upward past the beekeeper's hip toward about chest height.

Now I'm positioning the nozzle as a small cone angled forward-up from the lid, placing the smoke puffs just ahead of it so they clear the hand, and designing the smoker can itself as a lathe-shaped cylinder with a flared base, domed lid, bail pivot lugs, and black lacquer paint accented with red bands and gold decal stripes.

I'm figuring out where the smoker attaches in the rig -- adding a "smoker" joint parented off the wrist joint so it swings naturally from the arm, then checking the shoulder and arm chain parenting (shoulders off the chest joint, with shoulder spheres placed accordingly) and setting up L/R side naming conventions for the joints.

Now I'm writing the lacquer paint function, blending a base color with a cool shaded underside and a specular highlight based on light direction, then starting on the cream cloth paint function too.

The hem flares out like a lathe-turned shape, with the coat bottom at y=0.7 and a red band from .7-.775. I'm thinking about adding small gold dots along the hem using a ring of spheres at the widest torso point, maybe just a manual circle of dots instead of a more complex loop function.

For the trousers and boots, I'm planning cloth paint for trousers and black lacquer for the boots with a red band near the top. The boot shaft needs a lathe outline from bottom to top with a flare near the ankle cuff, and I'm considering building the cuff as a separate red ring loop so it reads as a distinct color band rather than blending into the black shaft.

Now I'm working out leg proportions relative to the boot — ankle sweep ending around y=0.1, boot shaft radius versus knee radius, trouser overlap above the cuff — then moving into the foot geometry, sizing the toe and sole ellipsoids to fit inside the boot's footprint.

I'm shaping the foot as a flattened ellipsoid sitting on the floor, adding a red sole band and a small gold toe cap for a decorative touch, then rigging the ankle bone for the boot. Next I'm starting on the sprig SVG texture, sketching a gold stem with curling leaves and red berries.

Still writing SVG curls...

Writing SVG panel template...

For the bee emblem I'm using a red circle with gold rim and a gold-bodied bee with black stripes and wings. For the face, I'm keeping the background transparent and remembering that low-opacity pixels get cut away, so instead of gradients I'm using solid rosy cheek discs with a two-tone red and pink ring, plus dark glossy eyes with white highlights and thick brown curved brows.

Now I'm placing the features: eyes at x=60/140 with white glints, cheeks at the sides sized around 13-14mm radius, thick arched brows above the eyes, and a small gold dot near the top like a cute bee accent, all scaled in millimeters to fit the sphere's decal width.

Next I'm sketching the mouth as a simple open smile with red fill and black outline, then designing the veil net pattern. For the honeycomb texture I'm drawing hexagonal cells against an amber background with darker outlines, some cells filled cream and others left dark gold with a soft glow for depth. I'm also planning smaller reusable elements like smoke puffs, a flower motif for the hat band, and a repeating berry-and-leaf border strip for the hive trims and hem details.

I'll apply the border strips to all four sides of each box rather than just front and back, stretching the pattern to fit varying widths since that's visually fine. That brings the texture list to nine total: sprig, panel A and B, border, emblem, face, mouth, veil, and honey.

Now I'm figuring out panel placement — box one gets panel A on a black background, box two gets panel B on red, with matching panels on the sides and back, while the top super box gets a window on its front instead. I'm sizing the panels to fit within the box height alongside the border strips, and adding thin gold corner posts to each box for visual detail.

Next I'm designing the hive stand: four tapered legs built via a lathe profile with red lacquer bodies and gold rings, positioned at the stand's corners, plus black cross-braces connecting them.

Then I'm working out the bottom board and box dimensions, sizing the board slightly wider than the hive boxes and extending forward to form a landing area, before adding an entrance slot and front panel detail to the lowest box.

I'm pinning down the hive's coordinate system, centering it symmetrically along z with the front face positioned, and starting to shape the gable roof with its overhanging eaves.

For the paint function, I'm deciding gable faces (where normal z is near vertical) get black lacquer with the emblem, while sloped roof faces get alternating gold and red stripes based on z-position, plus gold trim along the barge boards.

Now I'm adding decorative details: gold rod trim along the gable roof edges leading up to the apex, a gold finial knob at the ridge peak, and small gold spheres at the ridge ends. I'm also planning honey drip elements hanging from the front eave overhang, positioning them around the window opening with specific x-offsets to avoid overlapping the window itself.

Now I'm placing bees near the hive—around ten of them hovering in front and above, with a few on the landing board and near the beekeeper's veil, each given a position and heading vector. I'm also figuring out the smoker's position relative to the beekeeper's right hand, aligning its center with the wrist coordinate.

I'm now working out the bail wire's curved path over the smoker can, using a series of control points on either side that arc up to meet the handle bar, with the bar itself being a separate gold rod spanning the top.

Next I'm placing the spout: a red lacquered cone frustum rising from the lid toward a tip with a gold ring and glowing orange ember sphere inside, plus a starting point for smoke puffs drifting off the nozzle. Then I'm positioning the bellows attachment point along the side of the can, setting up where the boards will begin.

Now I'm shaping the bellows itself: a top and bottom board as flat boxes, kept horizontal rather than angled for simplicity, connecting to several thin accordion-fold boxes stacked at slightly varying widths and depths to mimic leather bellows, painted brown with mottled texture, while the boards get the same red lacquer and gold trim as the rest of the piece. I'm deciding to skip the nozzle tube and wire handle details for now to keep things manageable.

I also want to add a small flat gold-iron hive tool tucked into the sash, plus a bee motif on the hat brim and shoulder. Tallying up rough part counts across the hive, bees, and smoker gives me a budget around 300 parts, which feels reasonable with low triangle counts.

Setting up the builder scaffolding now...

Still building joint hierarchy...

Setting up the wrist as the arm's terminal joint, with finger chains parented to it, then computing hand geometry from the forearm direction vector.

I'm reconsidering the palm shape—switching from a box to a scaled sphere for a rounder, mitt-like look, then working out where the fingers should begin relative to that palm sphere's bounds.

Checking the finger path math against the bar circle radius to confirm the curled finger surface touches the bar surface correctly.

Now I'm working out the thumb joint positions, placing it on the medial side of the palm hugging the bar, with a simple two-joint chain and tapered radii.

For the fingers, I'm setting x-offsets based on index position with the pinky scaled down slightly, applying tapered sweep radii and the glove color along each chain, then moving on to lathe the gauntlet cuff around the forearm axis with a ring profile.

I'm working out a flaring quadrilateral cross-section for the cuff, with the wide end oriented toward the elbow and the narrow end at the wrist, computing the axis direction and offset point accordingly.

For coloring, I'm applying a lacquer-red base with a gold trim ring triggered by a height threshold in the paint function, keeping the sleeve cream overall but adding a scattered gold-dot decoration pattern to the upper sleeve.

I'll give the sleeves small red berry-like spots for a folk-fabric feel, while keeping the trousers and torso coat plain cloth to avoid clutter. I'm also placing small spherical shoulder joints near the sleeve start, since the rounded cap should cover the seam anyway.

Now I'm defining the torso sweep: a profile with radii tapering from hip to chest and back in toward the neck, swept along a straight catmull path from hips to neck height, using 14-sided circular cross-sections and bone-weighted to the spine and hips, with a flat cap at the bottom and rounded cap at the top.

I'm checking that the chest and neck segments connect correctly, with the neck tube continuing from the torso top using skin color since it'll be covered by a collar. Then I'm setting up the leg chains as symmetric limbs branching from the hips, with hip, knee, and ankle joints positioned along a catmull curve down each side.

Now I'm sweeping the trouser radii along those leg bones and confirming the legs stay visible below the coat's flat-bottomed hem, with the ankle joint marking where the boot shaft will attach.

Shaping the boot shaft as a lathe revolution with a tapered polygon outline, colored mostly black lacquer but with a red band and gold trim ring near the top. Then I'll move to building out the collar as a flared red lathe ring at the neck base, positioned to intersect naturally with the torso's sloped shoulder profile.

Still working out the sash geometry...

I'm placing a sprig decal on the chest and adjusting its vertical position so it doesn't overlap the sash below or the collar above, nudging the center to around y=1.17 to keep clean spacing.

I'm adding a matching sprig on the back and two smaller sprigs near the front hem flanking center, then considering small gold dot spheres distributed along the hem path for trim detail.

Right, since path points give tangent direction rather than a normal, using `stick` would orient wrong — better to place spheres with just position via a simpler part call. Then I'm planning a tassel hanging from the sash: a red knot sphere with several cord capsules dropping down, weighted to the hips bone.

For the hive tool, I'm sketching an L-shaped flat bar with a scraper end, positioning it tucked behind the sash near the left hip, oriented vertically so it sticks up slightly above the sash line.

Working out tool orientation...

I'll skip the chest emblem since it conflicts with the sprig placement, and instead reserve decals for the hat crown, hive roof, and smoker. Now I'm moving on to building the hat itself, starting with the lathe profile for the brim.

Writing brim lathe and paint shader...

Still working out the brim dot pattern...I'm also sketching the crown's lathe profile as a set of points defining the hat's curved silhouette.

For the hat itself, I'm setting black for the crown and a red band near the base, with gold trim, and placing an emblem decal on the crown front near the top. Finally I'm adding a small gold sphere knob at the very top of the crown.

Checking proportions: the crown top sits around y=1.765 which stays inside the skull dome, eyes at 1.575 clear the brim bottom near 1.60-1.64, and I'm adding a translucent veil cylinder (radius 0.30 top, 0.27 bottom, height 0.34) centered around y=1.47-1.48, tinted white, extending down to about y=1.30.

I'm confirming the veil's top edge at y=1.64 tucks neatly under the brim at radius 0.30, so it stays hidden within the brim's underside. The lattice pattern uses a textured material with alpha cutout for the net look, and I'm checking that the dark brown line color (#2a1a14) reads as "colored" rather than neutral gray so the mesh lines actually render visibly against the transparent base.

I'm now working out the veil's two trim rings—a thin gold tube loop near the top at y=1.64, r=0.30, and a thicker red tube loop at the bottom hem, y=1.31, r=0.27—built as closed Catmull-Rom circles swept into tube geometry with six-sided cross-sections. Then I add small skin-colored ear spheres positioned at the sides, visible below the brim, and I'm planning to add a few hair tufts near the sides to peek out from under the hat.

For the beard I'm placing bezier curve roots along the jaw at several angles, each starting lower on the face and curving down to varying lengths depending on angle—shortest at the sides, longest in the center—with control points pulling the curve outward and downward to shape it naturally.

Still writing beard geometry...

Attaching the mustache to the head bone, then adding a pink nose sphere also bound to the head. I'm setting up the decal system for face details and hive props, planning a `bee()` helper function for spawning bees attached to the hive joint, and starting a glow helper utility for visual effects.

Writing the glow function, handling both single-mesh parts and sweep-based parts with multiple meshes, making sure to clone materials safely and account for textured versus flat-colored surfaces.

Now I'm writing out SVG markup for a sprig-like plant shape, tracing its stem and leaf paths with dark outlines and a golden-yellow stroke layered on top for highlight detail.

Adding leaf and berry shapes...

Writing panel SVG generator...

Now I'm designing the flower center with rotated petals around a core circle, checking that the radius keeps everything within bounds, then moving to the border strip design with repeating berry-and-leaf units against a dark background.

For the emblem, I'm layering circles for a base and gold ring, then building a bee shape with a striped abdomen using a clipped ellipse and angled wing shapes on either side.

Now moving to the face, I'm curving brow strokes with quadratic paths and starting on eye ellipses.
